Items.Authors: Robin Swanson, Suresh Sivanandam
Items.Title: Post facto photon fixing
Items.Abstract: Single photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) have emerged as a potential successor of current wavefront sensor (WFS) and science camera detectors. Due to their lack of readout noise and ability to operate at very high frame-rates they are particularly well suited for low flux imaging -- as is often the case when observing with an adaptive optics (AO) system. However, while the underlying detector technologies are radically different, current applications of SPADs in AO settings have treated them simply as standard CMOS sensors with desirable noise properties. In this work we present a new method which takes advantage of the SPADs high-frame rates when used as a science camera. We show how by deconvolving science images using information from their associated residual WFS slopes, we can undo certain effects caused by servo-lag. We show that our method is capable of improving both Strehl ratio and contrast in simulation as well as preliminary experimental results.

Items.Authors: Daniel J. Patnaude, Ralph Kraft, Gerrit Schellenberger, Thomas Gauron, Paul Nulsen, Grant Tremblay, Bradley Bissell, Ken Gage, Matthew Dahmer
Items.Title: The Chandra X-ray Observatory high resolution camera: a 2026 status report
Items.Abstract: he High Resolution Camera (HRC) is one of the two prime instruments aboard the Chandra X-ray Observatory. It provides users with arcsecond imaging, microsecond timing resolution, and is the only active X-ray instrument with sensitivity to X-rays below the carbon edge. When combined with Chandra's insertable transmission gratings, the HRC offers resolving power > 1000 in the 70 - 200 eV band. Over its 25 year lifetime, the HRC has enabled transformative studies of neutron star kicks, superluminal jets, and the properties of exoplanet host stars. The Chandra HRC is now the benchmark for long duration studies of microchannel plates in a space environment. Here we discuss the current state of the HRC, including the operational status of the two cameras, the recovery efforts associated with two significant anomalies which have occurred in the last 5 years, and changes to HRC operations which have enabled its continued success.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Fulton, Jennifer Burt, Chad Bender, Andreas Quirrenbach, Andreas Seifahrt, Andrew Howard, Andy Szentgyorgyi, Cem Onyuksel, Chas Beichman, Damien Ségransan, Daniel Holdsworth, Emile Fontanet, Daniel M. Krolikowski, Étienne Artigau, Gaspare Lo Curto, Jonathan Crass, Julian Sturmer, Lars Buchhave, Leonardo Paredes, Lily Zhao, Marshall Johnson, Martino Romaniello, Megan Bedell, Michelle Edwards, Neil Cook, Rose Gibson, Sam Halverson, Sarah Logsdon, Sean Carey, Tanya Das, Xavier Dumusque, Timothy Pickering, Joris De Ridder, Saskia Prins
Items.Title: Developing a community EPRV data standard
Items.Abstract: The latest Extreme Precision Radial Velocity (EPRV) spectrographs have now collected enough data to study how instrument-specific hardware and software choices affect final RVs and stellar variability metrics. Our team has defined an EPRV data standard and 'translator' tools to enable cross-instrument comparisons and reveal previously hidden small-scale systematics. The standard also offers a starting point for new instruments, reducing the burden of developing independent formats and pipelines. We will present the first release, covering products from order-by-order spectra to derived RVs, along with translator templates that support coordinated comparisons of stellar data across EPRV spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Amélie Crebassa-Néron, Hélène T. Krol, Xavier Buet, Pierre-Louis Martin, Didier Torricini, Grégory Chauveau, Joost van den Born, Annemieke Janssen, Ester Aranzana
Items.Title: Narrow-band filters coatings for the cryogenic subsystem of the MICADO instrument
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the first-light near-infrared camera for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is designed to deliver unprecedented precision imaging for studies of galaxy evolution, the Galactic Center and its supermassive black hole, as well as the characterization of exoplanets and circumstellar disks. Installed under high vacuum and operated at cryogenic temperatures (~80 K), MICADO covers the 0.8–2.45 μm spectral range using two large filter wheels populated with broadband, intermediate-band, and narrow-band filters.  In the frame of this project, CILAS was in charge of the development of the narrow-band filter coatings. These filters must meet stringent optical and mechanical requirements to ensure high spectral stability and transmission in the cryogenic environment of the instrument.   We describe the design approach, coating technologies, and validation strategy implemented to guarantee performance at operating temperature.

Items.Authors: Frederic Lemmel, Vincent Affatato, Eloy Hernandez, Amitha Jha, Thibaut Prod'Homme, Malik Mansour, Benoit Serra, Elizabeth George
Items.Title: Pyxel 3.0: New features and applications for the collaborative instrument simulator
Items.Abstract: Pyxel is an open-source and collaborative Python-based framework for simulating imaging instruments with a strong focus on detector modelling. Pyxel version 3 introduces major enhancements, including preconfigured simulation pipelines for a catalogue of widely used detectors (e.g. Te2v CIS304, Leonardo IBEX, Teledyne HxRG) accessible through a new GUI, and support for focal-plane and multi-channel detector simulations.   With a rapidly growing community beyond the original ESA-ESO collaboration and contributions from CEA-Saclay, MSSL, CRAL and ISAE-Supaero, Pyxel is now used in numerous projects, including ESA’s Arrakihs mission.

Items.Authors: Kaitlyn Hessel, William Thompson, Sébastien Fabbro, Andre Fogal, Christopher Mann, Christian Marois, Adam Johnson, Olivier Lardière, Joeleff Fitzsimmons
Items.Title: On-sky coherent differential imaging with a self coherent camera: classical and machine learning pipelines
Items.Abstract: Coherent Differential Imaging (CDI) is a direct imaging post-processing technique that suppresses quasi-static speckles to isolate planetary signals. By exploiting the incoherence of planet and star light, CDI reconstructs the speckle field for subtraction, offering theoretically infinite contrast. Limitations in point spread function reconstruction and chromaticity constrain lab gains to ~30x using a Self Coherent Camera (SCC). We present the first on-sky CDI results with an SCC in the Subaru Pathfinder Instrument for Detecting Exoplanets and Retrieving Spectra (SPIDERS). We also investigate a machine learning (ML) approach to CDI to mitigate chromaticity and increasing contrast gains. These results demonstrate CDI’s capabilities on-sky with an SCC using both classical and ML pipelines, paving the way to deployment with the CAL2 system on the Gemini Planet Imager 2 and future development on the Habitable World’s Observatory, enabling detection of closer-in, lower-mass exoplanets.

Items.Authors: Giulia Conenna, Stephen Yates, Kenichi Karatsu, Anaïs Besnard, Valentin Sauvage, Daniela Perez Capelo, Dimitry Lamers, David Thoen, Martijn Veen, Jochem J. A. Baselmans, Lorenza Ferrari
Items.Title: Radiation qualification of lens-absorber and antenna-coupled kinetic inductance detectors for the PRIMA mission
Items.Abstract: Despite significant progress in far-infrared detector technology, demonstrating radiation hardness remains a critical step for space qualification. This is particularly relevant for the PRIMA mission, which require detectors capable of operating reliably over a decade in the L2 environment.  PRIMAger includes two KID designs: single-polarized leaky-lens antenna-coupled KIDs for the Polarimetric Imager (PPI), and lens-absorber-coupled KIDs for the Hyperspectral Imager (PHI). All devices are based on NbTiN resonators with an aluminum section for radiation absorption. PHI uses absorbers on solid Si, whereas PPI uses an aluminum coplanar waveguide coupled to an antenna fabricated on a 100 nm SiN membrane.  During the test campaign conducted at PARTREC (the Netherlands), our prototypes were cooled down in the DRACuLA cryostat to 120 mK and exposed to proton-beam radiation corresponding to the total dose expected over ten years at L2. The results show negligible degradation in key parameters.

Items.Authors: Bruce C. Bigelow, Chris Madden, Francisco Meza, Eduardo Villar, Miroslav Vulinovic
Items.Title: The GMT site, enclosure, and facilities: 2026 design and construction update
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) is one of three extremely large telescopes (ELTs) currently in design or construction. The GMT site is located on the summit of Cerro Las Campanas, a peak within the property of the Las Campanas Observatory (LCO) in Chile. The GMT employs seven 8.4m monolithic mirrors as segments to form a single optical surface with an equivalent diameter of 25.4 meters. Developing a new observatory for cutting-edge science operations and a 50-year lifespan poses a variety of design and construction challenges. This paper reports on progress since June, 2024, and addresses the latest developments for the GMT site master plan, completion of the enclosure design, final CFD modeling of the enclosure design, completion of the conceptual and preliminary design phases (and reviews) for the Summit Support Building, and design of the site infrastructure, including a detailed trade study for a ~5 Mega-Watt photo-voltaic power station and battery storage system.

Items.Authors: Jeffrey S. Smith, Lee D. Feinberg, John K. Ziemer
Items.Title: Habitable Worlds Observatory: project status
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory Technology Maturation Project Office (HWO-TMPO) is executing a comprehensive pre-formulation program to mature critical technologies and mission architectures for NASA's next flagship astrophysics mission following Roman. Established in August 2024 in response to the 2020 Decadal Survey's top large mission recommendation, HWO-TMPO has systematically progressed through Concept Maturity Levels while exploring multiple mission architectures via Exploratory Analytic Cases. The presentation will status across three primary technology development tracks: coronagraph systems, ultra-stable telescope technologies, and high-sensitivity UV/visible instrumentation.    This presentation will provide an overview of the technical and programmatic status on HWO-TMPO's progress toward Mission Concept Review.

Items.Authors: Hanshin Lee, Uma Subash, Menelaos K. Poutous
Items.Title: Reactive ion-plasma etched diffraction gratings for astronomy: production of science-grade 4x4 square inch gratings
Items.Abstract: We have been advancing the Reactive-Ion Plasma Etching (RIPLE) process for large surface-area fabrication of diffraction gratings for Astronomy. Earlier, we demonstrated the RIPLE process to be highly deterministic and presented near theoretical super-broadband diffraction efficiencies from several prototype 1x1 sq. inch RIPLE gratings. Standing upon this success, we forged ahead to scale the process to the primary 4x4 sq. inch target area. This areal scaling has been the core of the NSF-RIPLE program which was recently completed. The program’s main outcomes are the four copies of science-grade RIPLE gratings for the VIRUS2 instrument and demonstrates the mature RIPLE process that can result in deeply etched super-efficient large gratings for astronomical applications. In this paper, we describe the characteristics of these diffraction gratings and discuss some of the key methodologies, models, and measurements used in the scaling effort.

Items.Authors: Mark Wallace, Pascal Martinez
Items.Title: Procurement of the dome and the telescope structure of the ELT: update status report
Items.Abstract: The telescope Main Structure and the Dome of the ELT are being procured by ESO as an integrated system together with the auxiliary building and the service plants and are supplied by the ACe Consortium. The contract was signed in May 2016 and the road to completion is long and winding and paved on all sides with pitfalls. The progress is visible and tangible; the primary and secondary structures are complete, and we are nearing completion of the physical installations (e.g. electrical, and fluid distribution), with commissioning just around the corner. However, there are various challenges yet to be overcome. In this paper we will describe the progress and achievements of the project so far as well as give an outline of the obstacles still on the horizon.

Items.Authors: Claire Poppett, David J. Schlegel, Arjun Dey, Klaus Honscheid, Paul Martini, Alex Drlica-Wagner, Pat Jelinsky, Chang-Jin Oh, Konstantina Boutsia, Joseph H. Silber, Nicholas R. Wenner
Items.Title: Spec-S5: a next-generation all-sky spectroscopic facility enabling large-scale surveys for cosmology and astrophysics
Items.Abstract: The Stage-5 Spectroscopic Experiment (Spec-S5) is a next-generation, all-sky spectroscopic facility designed to address fundamental questions in cosmology and astrophysics. Building on the legacy of DESI, Spec-S5 will upgrade two existing 4-m telescopes into 6-m wide-field observatories, each equipped with a highly multiplexed spectrograph capable of measuring 13,000 spectra simultaneously. This overview paper summarizes the science motivation, system architecture, and integration strategy of the project. Spec-S5 will deliver a more than tenfold increase in spectroscopic capability, enabling transformative surveys in the post-Rubin, post-DESI era and advancing our understanding of dark matter, dark energy, and cosmic structure formation.

Items.Authors: Marco Landoni, Giorgio Calderone, Paolo Di Marcantonio, Manuel Monteiro, Alessio Zanutta, Livia Origlia, Elena Mason, Roberto Cirami, Veronica Baldini, Andrea Balestra, Igor Coretti, Guido Cupani, Vincent Geers, Arto Jarvinen, Adrian Kaminski, Jorg Knoche, Jochen Liske, Mike Macintosh, Madhusudan Malve, Thomas Marquart, Alessandro Marconi, Matteo Porru, Nicoletta Sanna, Andrea Scaudo, Danuta Sosnowska
Items.Title: ANDES, the high resolution spectrograph for the ELT: the Instrument Control Software
Items.Abstract: In this paper, we present a comprehensive overview of the Instrument Control Software architecture designed for the ArmazoNes high Dispersion Echelle Spectrograph (ANDES), developed as part of the preparation for the instrument’s Preliminary Design Review (PDR). The ANDES Control Software is based on the European Southern Observatory (ESO) Instrument Control System Framework (IFW\cite{ifw}). In this manuscript we focus on the architectural choices required to fully support the operation of a highly distributed instrument such as ANDES for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). We describe the strategies foreseen for the design, development, and deployment of both the low-level control software, dedicated to hardware and device management, and the high-level control software, responsible for coordinating the observations. Furthermore, we detail how the different detectors will be controlled.

Items.Authors: John D. Monnier
Items.Title: Development of quantum technologies for optical/infrared interferometry
Items.Abstract: Quantum technologies may revolutionize optical interferometry through new means to distribute and preserve electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. After reviewing existing techniques, I survey proposed quantum-sensing and quantum-networking applications and highlight recent laboratory demonstrations of key building blocks. By easing field-transport demands for baselines beyond ~1 km, quantum-enhanced interferometry could enable µas-class astrometry and imaging relevant to exoplanets and supermassive black hole environments.    That said, "going quantum" is not a magic shortcut to sensitivity because many of the most compelling science cases remain photon- and turbulence-limited. I therefore emphasize the practical constraints -- loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength limits of quantum interfaces -- that must also be overcome to make these capabilities useful for astronomy, whether deployed on the ground or from space.

Items.Authors: Stuart D. Bale
Items.Title: LuSEE-Night: A low lrequency radio pathfinder for the lunar farside
Items.Abstract: The NASA/DOE LuSEE Night experiment [Bale et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.10345] will be deployed on the lunar farside in late 2026 to make full-Stokes spectral measurements of the radio sky below 50 MHz using a simple crossed-dipole antenna system. LuSEE Night will be a pathfinder for future farside observatories, demonstrating many of the (quite ambitious) technologies required to make synoptic, radio quiet measurements throughout the lunar night. A ’stretch’ goal of LuSEE Night is the first measurement of the 21cm spectral features associated with very high redshift (z~100) universe. The foregrounds to this signal will be dominant by several orders of magnitude but offer their own novel scientific opportunities

Items.Authors: David Schiminovich, Nicole D. Melso, Meghna Sitaram, Ignacio Cevallos Aleman, Erika T. Hamden
Items.Title: Narrowband integral field spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry: current capabilities and future prospects with advanced optical designs, metamaterials and detectors
Items.Abstract: We present design concepts and prototype performance of next-generation technologies for narrowband integral field spectrographs (NB-IFS) with moderate to high velocity resolution (R ~10,000–40,000), engineered to push extremely low–surface brightness emission detection to new limits. Building on the recent deployment of CHαS—the Circumgalactic H-alpha Spectrograph on the MDM 2.4m telescope—we are advancing NB-IFS concepts for ground- and space-based platforms that challenge assumptions of conventional design. Several concepts replace core components—including the filter, slicer, collimator, grating, and camera—with optical metasurfaces, effectively reimagining the CHαS IFU as a narrowband, highly dispersive, wavelength-routing metalens array. Some also provide full-Stokes spectropolarimetric separation. We compare these to state-of-the-art systems and outline a path to sensitivity gains using photon-counting detectors and, further ahead, non-local Fourier-filtering metasurfaces.

Items.Authors: Roberto Neri, Karl Friedrich Schuster
Items.Title: NOEMA in the wideband era - dual-band receivers and full-stokes polarimetry
Items.Abstract: NOEMA is the most sensitive millimeter/submillimeter interferometer in the northern hemisphere, offering high sensitivity, high resolution imaging across 70–373 GHz. The new Dual-Band upgrade enables full sensitivity observations of 7.7 GHz IF bandwidth per polarization and sideband simultaneously in both the 3 and 1 mm bands. The two identical advanced wideband correlators PolyFiX 1 and 2 deliver 62 GHz of instantaneous complete high-resolution spectral coverage. This crucially accelerates line surveys, provides high precision continuum measurements for SED determinations, reduces calibration systematics through band-to-band phase referencing, and opens new possibilities for transient astrophysics. A major new capability is full-Stokes polarimetry, with Band 1 foreseen for general users in 2026. NOEMA enables spatially resolved studies of magnetic fields, astrochemistry, star and planet formation, and galaxy evolution.

Items.Authors: Roberta Zanin, Volker Heinz, Bernhard Lopez, David Green, David Green, Paolo G. Calisse, Markus Gaug, Michele Doro, Matthias Füssling, Igor Oya, Andrea Cremonini, Vanessa Montes, Orel Gueta, Mieke Bouwhuis, Maurizio Miccolis, Paolo Petrinca
Items.Title: Operating the CTAO: Challenges of a Distributed VHE gamma-ray observatory
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is a next-generation, open and proposal-driven facility for very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy, operating as an observatory with four places of operation in Italy, Germany, Spain, and Chile. Approaching the deployment of its first intermediate array configuration, the CTAO will soon exceed the performance of current instruments and begin early science operations while progressing toward its baseline configuration. This paper outlines CTAO end-to-end workflow, from proposal preparation and observation planning to data processing and delivery of science-ready products. It highlights the coordination required across its hemispheric stations to optimize scientific return, enable rapid response to transient events, and support MWL and MM studies. A fully integrated atmospheric characterization program ensures control of systematic uncertainties, while tightly coupled technical and scientific operations maintain long term performance.

Items.Authors: Matthew R. Bolcar, Feng Zhao, Paul Scowen, Lee Feinberg, Jeffrey S. Smith, Josh Abel
Items.Title: The Habitable Worlds Observatory technology development plan
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory is NASA’s next large space telescope, selected by the 2020 Decadal Survey in Astronomy and Astrophysics to search for and characterize habitable exoplanets while enabling a broad range of transformative astrophysics. The HWO Technology Maturation Project Office (TMPO) is exploring the HWO science, technology, and mission architectures toward a Mission Concept Review (MCR) at the end of the decade. A primary deliverable of this effort is a technology development plan that identifies critical technologies that enable the mission, defines a process for assessing the readiness of those technologies, and outlines a strategy for developing those technologies to a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 5 before the MCR. In this paper we summarize the HWO technology development plan which comprises three “tracks”: Coronagraph System technologies, Ultra-stable Telescope System technologies, and High-sensitivity Ultraviolet and Visible Instrumentation technologies.

Items.Authors: Amirhossein Kermani, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Matteo Genoni, Marco Riva, Alessio Zanutta, Michèle R. Lavagna
Items.Title: Towards AI-assisted AstroMBSE: building a knowledge corpus from SysML models and TLRs
Items.Abstract: In recent years, Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has been successfully applied to the design of astronomical instruments thanks to the AstroMBSE framework. However, current practice still relies heavily on manual work to manage the system, and many key activities – such as deriving functional architectures and physical breakdowns from top-level requirements (TLRs) – are still performed by hand, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. In this study, we present the first step towards an AI-assisted AstroMBSE co-pilot: the construction of a structured knowledge corpus from existing AstroMBSE projects. The corpus created in this initial phase will be used as a reusable resource for future work and will support later studies on how to use AI to propose operational scenarios and functional architectures, and to check the quality of system models.

Items.Authors: Konstantin B. Holzner, Christopher Renkl, Manuel Brekenfeld, Dominik Lentrodt, Leonid P. Yatsenko, Alexander Richter, Sebastian Hepp, Georg Heinze, Tobias Meyer, Andreas Amarotico, Philipp Putzer, Alexander Niggebaum, Bernward Dimke, Martin Enderlein, Bernhard Ernstberger, Armin Zach, Guillaume Bourdarot, Helmut Feuchtgruber, Frank Eisenhauer, Lauren H. Schatz, Steven M. Massey, Robert L. Johnson, Domenico Bonaccini Calia, Frank Lison
Items.Title: Return flux measurements of a high-power polychromatic laser guide star
Items.Abstract: Laser guide star (LGS) adaptive optics has become widespread in ground-based astronomy. It is also the most promising approach for countering atmospheric distortions in uplink optical satellite communications and laser-based space debris tracking and manoeuvring. The best performance is achieved when the LGS is created in the sodium layer at 90 km altitude. A major shortcoming of the technique is the tip/tilt indeterminacy of the LGS, which requires an additional reference beacon (natural guide star or satellite downlink), limiting sky coverage or the control of uplink beam wander. We report on recent simulations and on-sky experiments exploring the feasibility of a polychromatic LGS, which enables tip/tilt measurement via the differential tilt between two wavelengths emitted by the sodium guide star. For the experiments, we have used two state-of-the-art > 50-W laser systems at 589 and 569 nm, based on TOPTICA’s second-generation guide star laser platform.

Items.Authors: Samuel Park, Keath Beifus, Colby Gottschalk, Nick Juelsgaard, King-Ming Lam, Nathan Loewen, Byron Smith, William Burgett, Jeff Kimberly, Dave Zarembski, Giovanni Bonomi, Todd Trieloff, Volker Grimm, Dietmar Koch, Eberhard Sust, Ulrich Weis, Peter Eisenträger, Konstantinos Giannouloudis, Benjamin Hauska, Alexei Ippa, Aleksej Kiselev, Sebastian Lüft, Alexander Rohr, Lehel Simeny, Raffaele Tomelleri
Items.Title: The Giant Magellan Telescope Mount: manufacturing progress of the azimuth systems
Items.Abstract: The GMTO Mount is being assembled and tested at the Ingersoll Machine Tools (IMT) factory in Rockford, Illinois. All three motion axes and critical systems will be functionally tested before being shipped and installed at the GMT Las Campanas site in Chile. The large steel fabrication of the Azimuth Track and Azimuth rotating disk structure are nearly complete. The Azimuth mechanisms including the Hydrostatic Bearing System, Earthquake Damping System, drives, and utility wrap are in process of being assembled. Significant design and optimization of the utilities system including power distribution, coolant, and fiber communication have been completed.

Items.Authors: Stephen P. Todd, Éamonn Harvey, Anna MacIver, William Taylor, Eduard Muslimov, Kjetil Dohlen, Matthias Tecza, Magali Loupias, Paula Bañares, Mark Swinbank, Ryan Griffiths
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: line spread functions in a diffraction limited spectrometer
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.   Diffraction of the pupil becomes significant in a spectrograph where the slit width is comparable to the diffraction limited PSF. When the spatial coherence due to the narrow slit is considered, the resulting line spread function can be narrower than the geometric width of the input slit, with a non-linear dependence on the size of the pupil aperture after the slit. We outline the impact of these diffraction and spatial filtering effects on the line spread function of HARMONI and identify parameters that should be considered when designing a diffraction limited spectrograph.

Items.Authors: P. Petrinca, A. Cremonini, M. Rossi, D. Simone, R. Zanin
Items.Title: Bridging science, design, and verification: a model-based architecture for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) implements a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) framework to bridge scientific objectives with system design and verification. This paper details a SysML-based process where the system architecture is derived directly from Science Use Cases, establishing a single Source of Truth. Behavioral modeling is shown to not only generate unambiguous requirements but also support a "Design-Driven" Verification and Validation (V&V) strategy. By mapping behavioral paths directly to test scenarios, complete traceability from scientific goals to test procedures is ensured. This approach facilitates early verification planning, reduces integration risks, and optimizes costs by validating operational logic prior to physical implementation.

Items.Authors: Reinhardt von Brandis-Martini, Tinus Stander
Items.Title: Concept designs for concurrent quad-band sideband separating downconverters
Items.Abstract: Simultaneous observation at multiple frequencies improves radio telescope efficiency by  increasing the data collected per unit observation time, and enables frequency-phase-transfer  (FPT) calibration of VLBI observations. The Korean VLBI network (KVN) represents the  state of the art in concurrent multi-band observation, and employs a quasi-optical front-end.  This solution requires significant cabin volume and duplication of receiver components. We  investigate two multi-mixer topologies to extend a standard sideband separating (2SB) mixer  to a quad-band sideband separating (4SB) downconverter. The resulting image rejection ratios  of 10 dB and conversion loss of 15–20 dB indicate a solution that offers a compact and power-  efficient alternative to a quasi-optical system.

Items.Authors: Julienne Boettger, Ronald Holzlöhner, Felipe Pedreros Bustos, Szymon Gladysz, Pierre Haguenauer, David Jenkins, Christian Fruck, Thomas Pfrommer
Items.Title: Error budget for tip/tilt retrieval from laser guide stars using the Propagation-Delay Method
Items.Abstract: The Propagation-Delay Method proposes that atmospheric tip/tilt can be retrieved from a residual laser guide star (LGS) tip/tilt that arises due to the evolving atmospheric turbulence between the laser uplink and LGS downlink. Even partial recovery of tip/tilt from LGS could already increase integration times on natural guide stars, potentially enabling full sky coverage. However, this differential LGS tip/tilt is expected to be 2–3 orders of magnitude smaller than the NGS tip/tilt and thus could be swamped by noise. We analyse noise and error contributions in the detection process, as well as sensitivity limits for the tip/tilt detection with Shack-Hartmann and pyramid wavefront sensors. Finally, we obtain an error budget by comparing the derived noise contributions with the expected signal power spectra under different turbulence and LGS launch conditions, along with the corresponding signal-to-noise ratio as a function of the relevant system parameters.

Items.Authors: Paul A. Scowen, Kevin France, Chris Packham, Richard Cartwright, Janice Lee, Evgenya Shkolnik, Allison Youngblood, Jonathan Papa, Joseph Howard, Breann Sitarski, Jason Tumlinson, Alice Liu, Aki Roberge, Grace Sweetak, Brian Fleming, Guangjun Gao
Items.Title: HWO UV instrument studies: bounding conditions and interfaces
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) Technology Maturation Project Office (HTMPO) released a call in 2026 for US-led instrument studies. The instrument concepts should be designed to meet the transformative astrophysics measurement capabilities defined by the Community Science and Instrumentation Team (CSIT) in their analysis of science cases developed by the international astronomical community. The instrument study call defined bounding conditions such as mass, power and volume, as well as a fundamental understanding of the optical, mechanical and thermal interfaces provided by the latest two observatory design concepts. The ultraviolet instrument (UVI) coordination team developed these bounding conditions in 2025 – 2026 with a view to the likely range of capabilities for those instruments. While the NASA-sponsored instrument study call focuses on US-led proposals, NASA fully supports collaborative efforts for instrument studies and designs from international partners.

Items.Authors: Amanda Ibsen, Michael Reuter, Angelo Fausti, Tiago Ribeiro
Items.Title: Making sense of metrics: monitoring the performance of the Rubin Observatory Control System
Items.Abstract: The Rubin Observatory Control System coordinates many distributed components. Observability platforms have been set up to provide raw metrics, dashboards, and logs, but turning that information into operational understanding requires continuous monitoring and analysis.  This work focuses on how the observatory software team monitors the health and performance of the Control System during operations. Through real-life examples, we present the metrics that have proven most useful for diagnosing issues and discuss how cross-system dashboards and alerts support rapid fault localization and resolution.  Rather than detailing the observability stack itself, this work concentrates on practical use: how metrics guide investigation, how interpretations evolve with experience, and how this accumulated experience ultimately improves the reliability of a highly complex real-time telescope control system.

Items.Authors: Michael Schubnell, Tim Fanning, Andrew Hope, Joseph Silber, Greg Tarlé, Nicholas Wenner
Items.Title: A hybrid r–theta fiber positioning robot using a piezoelectric bender for radial motion
Items.Abstract: We present a novel R-Theta fiber positioner for next-generation spectroscopic instruments, addressing the dense array and fine-pitch needs of future dark energy surveys like Spec-S5. Our hybrid design decouples the two axes: Theta (rotation) uses a compact gearmotor, while radial (R) movement is achieved via a piezoceramic bender. This enables compact packaging, rapid and accurate closed-loop positioning, minimal interference, and cost efficiency. Closed-loop control uses a fiber view camera and centroid algorithm to counter piezo actuator creep and hysteresis. Prototype tests demonstrate micron-level accuracy and reliability at 2-second feedback intervals, showing strong scalability for the fiber densities required by Spec-S5.

Items.Authors: Thomas M. Herbst, Markus Feldt, Pascal Birckigt, Reinhard Geiß, Matthias Goy, Stefan Risse, Silvia Scheithauer, Uwe D. Zeitner
Items.Title: A hybrid grism for efficient space-based slitless spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We describe our efforts to design and test an entirely new class of optical device for slitless spectroscopy from space. By using nanostructured hybrid gratings, we can devote a fraction (typically 10%) of the telescope pupil to direct imaging, with the remainder allocated to spectroscopy. This permits simultaneous measurement of the “ground-truth” image and the dispersed light, and it allows flexible placement of the image and spectrum on a single detector. We report on our progress using two different approaches: 1. Integration of monolithic prisms onto lithographic gratings using robotic and interferometrically-controlled alignment systems; and 2. Production of nano-gratings and micro-prisms directly on a wafer using lithography only. The eventual goal is to produce at least two prototypes that we can test in the lab and at a ground-based observatory.

Items.Authors: Trupti M. Ranka, Bo Xin, Martin Hubert, Dave S. Ashby, Chris Contaxis, Michael Tuell, William Hubler, Barbara Fischer, Michael Gardiner, Gary Muller, Jose Soto, Neill Mills, Austin Everman, Dave Zeller, John Ford, Tommy Salanski, Tomas Krasuski
Items.Title: GMT Primary Mirror Test Cell Performance and Optical Testing Results
Items.Abstract: The GMT project designed and built a full-scale prototype of its 8.4-meter primary mirror segment active support system and the thermal control system called the “Test Cell”. One of the 7 primary mirror segments was tested with the test cell to demonstrate the performance of the active support system and thermal control system before committing to its production for all seven of the 8.4-meter diameter primary mirror segments. Detailed tests were performed to show the performance of the active support and thermal system and their ability to control the optical surface shape. This paper presents the results of the extensive test campaign. It shows that the system meets all the key requirements despite a few challenges.

Items.Authors: Christiaan D. Brinkerink, Nathalie Boudin, Nikolaos Sarantinos, Sonia Ghosh, Léon Koopmans, César Gómez-Hernández, Roel Jordans, Marc Klein Wolt, Barbara Matyjasiak, Tomasz Mis, Marek Morawski, Lukasz Nowak, Jacob Pasqualotto, David Prinsloo, Hanna Rothkaehl, Mark Ruiter, Anchal Saxena, Jan Tauber, Antonio Vecchio
Items.Title: Making Moon-based neutral hydrogen cosmology possible: current technology development towards the Dark-ages EXplorer (DEX)
Items.Abstract: The design and development of an instrument that can perform neutral hydrogen cosmology from the lunar far side presents a wide range of technical challenges, which is why current efforts of the Astrophysical Lunar Observatory topical team (ALO TT) focus on the development of technology that will make such a system possible. This includes ultra-low mass antenna systems, novel antenna deployment systems, temperature-tolerant electronics and low-power signal processing. In this contribution, I give an overview of the ongoing technology maturation efforts as well as the next steps in this larger context. These concrete efforts include the development of foil-based antenna systems and novel approaches to low-power radio receiver hardware.

Items.Authors: Robert W. Goodrich, William S. Burgett, Aline Souza, Chris Echols, Frank Hassell, Keath Beifus, Colby Gottschalk, Chris Madden
Items.Title: Operations planning for the Giant Magellan Telescope
Items.Abstract: The GMT is one of the extremely large ground-based OIR telescopes being designed and built. Operations planning includes developing behaviors (aka use cases) describing observatory operations/maintenance. Behaviors describe operational processes given the current knowledge of the design, and evolve along with that design. Behaviors are used to: identify weak spots in the design; develop hazard analyses; estimate technical staff resources required for operations and maintenance.    We also describe the transition from the construction stage through commissioning into early and then steady-state operations. We identify roles in the current project plan that will carry over into operations, creating a smooth transition between the stages and discuss how costs from operations and maintenance will be segregated from construction costs.    Plans for “early operations” (the first five years after construction) are presented, and the components for the steady-state operations budget outlined.

Items.Authors: Joshua Collier, John Wallis, Elrina Hartman, David Gozzard
Items.Title: Quantum-optimal optical interferometers for high-resolution astronomy
Items.Abstract: Recent advances in quantum information theory have led to the development of quantum imaging methods that provide imaging sensitivities and resolutions surpassing what can be achieved by conventional cameras and interferometers. These techniques have the potential to create optical interferometer telescopes with baselines of hundreds of kilometers and achieve resolutions on the order of 1 microarcsecond.    We present results of laboratory experiments advancing quantum interferometer techniques for astronomy. We demonstrate quantum-optimal imaging of an artificial star-like source using a phase-stabilized 170km-span optical interferometer, pointing the way to astronomical interferometers with resolution orders of magnitude better than any current telescope, with outstanding applications for studying exoplanets, the formation of star systems, and tests of General Relativity near the event horizon of a black hole.

Items.Authors: Noelia Martínez Rey
Items.Title: First high-resolution IFU observations of the sodium layer: implications for LGS tip–tilt sensing
Items.Abstract: Sodium Laser Guide Stars are created by exciting mesospheric Na atoms with a 589 nm laser. While the vertical sodium profile is well studied for AO, its horizontal structure remains largely unexplored. Gravity waves can produce long-lived Na density variations that may provide a new way to retrieve atmospheric tip-tilt from LGS. We present a feasibility study using the KOALA IFU and AAOmega spectrograph at the Anglo-Australian Telescope to resolve small-scale Na structures. With 1.25″ sampling and a 27.4″ × 50.6″ field of view (≈54 cm resolution at 90 km), we target the faint Na I airglow using the 670 nm dichroic and 580V grating, with 10–40 min sky exposures. We assess the detectability and stability of mesospheric Na features and evaluate their potential as wide-field tracers for separating uplink and downlink tip-tilt in LGS AO systems.

Items.Authors: Vincent Pelzer, Sebastian Egner, Constanza Fiedler, Sergio González, Robert Hamilton, Matias Jaeger, Juan Millar, Marcos Ortega, Liga Marija Putna, Michele Zamparelli, Erich Zehl
Items.Title: A structured approach using MBSE to implement a new CMMS system for ESO Observatories
Items.Abstract: The European Southern Observatory (ESO) is continuously advancing its technological infrastructure to meet the evolving demands of modern astronomical research and the operation of next-generation facilities such as the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). A critical component of this effort is the introduction of a new Computerized Maintenance Management System (CMMS) for its observatories.    The implementation of such a system is inherently complex, given its integration with numerous other software tools, data sources, and diverse stakeholders across multiple sites. To address this complexity, a structured approach is essential. In this paper, we detail our methodology applying the principles of the Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) and using MagicDraw to model business processes and data flows, capture use cases and requirements, perform testing and prototyping for early validation, and followed by the verification of user requirements.

Items.Authors: Dominik Neise, Pierre Aubert, Gabriele Barni, Pedro Bauza, David Berge, Jan-Philipp Bolle, Wahib Boulakbech, Pietro Bruno, Uros Bajc, Andrea Bulgarelli, Massimo Cappi, Franca Cassol, Sami Caroff, Luca Castaldini, Tiffany Collins, Vito Conforti, Alessandro Costa, Ludovic David, Giovanni De Cesare, Emma de Ona Wilhelmi, Ambra Di Piano, Kathrin Egberts, Rodrigo Fernandez, Valentina Fioretti, Hasmik Gasparyan, Stefano Germani, Jim Hinton, Federico Incardona, Dmitriy Kostunin, Bernhard Lopez, Etienne Lyard, Gilles Maurin, David Melkumyan, Enrique Mestre, Kevin Munari, Thomas Murach, Adam Muraczewski, Nariman Nakhjiri, Thibaut Oprinsen, Igor Oya, Gabriele Panebianco, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Emmanuel Pietriga, Vincent Pollet, Bronislaw Rudak, Iftach Sadeh, Sunil Sah, Marc Schefer, Torsten Schmidt, David Soldevila, Sebastiano Spinello, Constantin Steppa, Diego F. Torres, Andrea Tramacere, Ramon Valles Puig, Thomas Vuillaume, Roland Walter, Felix Werner, Arne Wörheide
Items.Title: Architectural design and operational progress of the ACADA system for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Array Control and Data Acquisition (ACADA) system is the central software platform enabling on-site operations of the CTAO. Built on the ACS framework, it coordinates control of more than sixty telescopes and auxiliary instruments, integrating supervision, data acquisition, scheduling, alert handling, and real-time analysis. Following its first major release and validation with LST-1, ACADA has passed its Critical Design Review and is progressing toward Release 2, which extends end-to-end operational capabilities, enhances resource supervision, improves observation workflows, strengthens monitoring and alarm handling, and upgrades the Science Alert Generation pipeline. Its integration has been validated through continuous integration, distributed test clusters, and on-site campaigns. This contribution presents the architecture, operational experience, and ongoing developments preparing ACADA for multi-telescope operations at CTAO-North and CTAO-South.

Items.Authors: Kevin C. France, Janice Lee, Eric Burns, Jason Tumlinson, Chris Packham, Evgenya Shkolnik, Aki Roberge, Paul Scowen
Items.Title: HWO key science and instrument goals for UV imaging and spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: This talk summarizes current progress by the HWO Community Science and Instrumentation Team (CSIT) to identify and quantify science cases that motivate the capabilities of the UV instrument suite for HWO. Key science drivers currently include the regulation of star formation over cosmic time through galactic feedback, the intergalactic ionizing radiation field, the properties of the first stars, and the evolution of chemical complexity in stars and galaxies, and access to ozone in the atmospheres of potentially habitable planets. We describe select science cases as well as the measurement goals and instrument capabilities they imply for the HWO, ranging from UV high-resolution point-source spectroscopy, multi-object and integral field spectroscopy, and far-UV imaging capabilities. The talk will conclude with a synthesis of these measurement capabilities and a description of the next steps for UV instrument definition through the 2026 call for US HWO instrument studies.

Items.Authors: Victor Belitsky, Igor Lapkin, Alexey Pavolotsky, François Joint, Denis Meledin, Erik Sundin, Leif Helldner, Magnus Strandberg, Mathias Fredrixon, Sven-Erik Ferm, Vincent Desmaris
Items.Title: Wideband dual-polarization 2SB receiver for space and ground applications around 1mm wavelength
Items.Abstract: We present the latest results in the development of a wideband 2SB SIS mixer that covers RF band 210-375 GHz with an IF band 4-20 GHz. This mixer and receiver based on this mixer have a wide range of applications starting from single-dish observations, e.g., APEX SEPIA, potentially in ngEHT project and space VLBI. The SIS mixer features an integrated IF circuitry implemented on alumina substrate with Nb superconducting transmission lines and comprising IF matching components, IF/DC bias-T and IF 90-degree 3 dB hybrid. The mixer employs SIS junctions produced in-house with tunnel barrier made of AlN and having junction area about 2 µm2 in the twin configuration with RnA =14 Ω•µm2. The tested noise performance of the SIS receiver with this mixer in combination with OMT, corrugated feed and optics optimized for an RF band corresponding to ALMA Band 6 and ALMA Band 7 demonstrates the noise temperature of about x4 quantum noise hf/k SSB with sideband rejection above10 dB.

Items.Authors: Cole Meyer, Joanne Flores, Jason Corliss, Walter Harris
Items.Title: Characterization of a symmetric-facet dual-ruled grating for spatial heterodyne spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Dual-bandpass spatial heterodyne spectrometers (DB-SHS) enable simultaneous high-resolution measurements of spectral line pairs for astrophysical and planetary diagnostics. Unlike single-bandpass SHS instruments, DB-SHS requires an incident beam to straddle two adjacent diffraction gratings so each beam half interacts with a distinct ruling density and blaze angle. Using physically separate gratings prevents the high-precision optical co-alignment required for SHS instruments. Dual-ruled gratings solve this by integrating multiple ruled sections onto a single substrate, drastically reducing the alignment degrees of freedom. In this talk, I will describe recent efforts to characterize the diffraction efficiency of this novel dual-ruled grating. This work lays the foundation for laboratory validation of the first DB-SHS, ultimately enabling high-resolution spectroscopy of critical spectral line pairs.

Items.Authors: David Lee, Joël Vernet, Roland Bacon, Alexandre Jeanneau, Corentin Cudennec, Olga Bellido-Tirado, Roelof S. de Jong, Andreas Kelz, Steve Watson, Younes Chahid, Chris Waring, Laura Gibbs, Anmol Goyal, Dave Melotte, Lawrence Bissell, Sébastien Pernecker, Maxime Rombach, Malak Galal, Jonathan Wei, Aaron Omadutt, Jean-Paul Kneib, Joseph Barrow, Jon Lawrence, Will Saunders, Dimitri Buffat, Kjetil Dohlen, Andrea Tozzi, Anna Brucalassi, Matteo Munari, Simone D'Auria, Maria Sofia Randich, Jan W. Kragt, Ramon Navarro, Thomas Augusteijn, Andrea Bianco, Elizabeth M. George, Omar Sqalli, Olaf Iwert, Alessandro Meoli, Christophe Yèche , Christophe Magneville, Etienne Burtin, Julia Bryant, Philippe Dierickx, Paolo Franzetti, Vincenzo Mainieri, Jay Stephan, Oscar Gonzalez
Items.Title: WST, the wide-field spectroscopic telescope: progress on the design of the instruments
Items.Abstract: WST – the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope is a proposed new facility that will provide a transformational gain in spectroscopic survey capability over existing facilities. The WST is a 12 metre class telescope equipped with instrumentation to provide simultaneous observations in both multiple-object spectroscopy and integral field spectroscopy modes. This paper will describe the status of the instruments being designed for the WST, the fibre positioner module, the low and high-resolution multiple object spectrographs, the integral field spectrograph, disperser technology, sustainable detector and cryostat technology, and the calibration system. An overview of the overall layout of the instruments within the WST facility will be provided

Items.Authors: Grace Piroscia, Julien Lozi, Sébastien Vievard, Miles Lucas, Adam Taras, Peter Tuthill, Steve Ertel, Olivier Guyon, Vincent Deo
Items.Title: Full-pupil aperture masking with Jewel: high-sensitivity imaging and wavefront sensing
Items.Abstract: Now over 150 years old, aperture masking interferometry (AMI) remains a leading technique for high angular resolution optical astronomy. Despite this success, AMI faces intrinsic limitations from the requirement of non-redundancy, typically resulting in throughputs of 10% or less and poor spatial coverage. The Jewel aperture mask overcomes these limitations by encoding multiple non-redundant (NR) patterns onto a single optic, fully tiling the pupil with sub-apertures. Beyond high-efficiency masking, the full-pupil NR sampling provided by Jewel allows for the robust measurement of the underlying wavefront structure, enabling Jewel to act simultaneously as a science instrument and a wavefront sensor. We demonstrate the integration of Jewel into a multi-sensor adaptive optics system on SCExAO at Subaru, correcting low-order residual wavefront errors such as the low-wind effect and introduce a newly fabricated Jewel for the Large Binocular Telescope, paving the way for an ELT-scale design.

Items.Authors: Oliver Pfuhl, Jose Antonio Abad, Constanza Araujo-Hauck, Jean-Paul Kirchbauer, Helen Bedigan, Henri Bonnet, Martin Brinkmann, Elsa Calmette, Greidy Castellanos, Angela Cortes, Byron Engler, Michael Esselborn, Christoph Frank, Fernando Gago, Eduardo Garces, Elizabeth George, Thomas Grudzien, Ivan Guidolin, Andreas Haimerl, Peter Hammersley, Marcus Haug, Stefan Huber, Paul Jolley, Aglaé Kellerer, Manuel Kern, Petr Janout, Mario Kiekebusch, Barbara Klein, Johannes Kolmeder, Johan Kosmalski, David Kosten, Paolo La Penna, Ulrich Lampater, Serban Leveratto, Steffan Lewis, Christopher Mandla, Enrico Marchetti, Leander Mehrgan, Christophe Moins, Jérôme Paufique, Lorenzo Pettazzi, Thomas Pfrommer, Adam Rubin, Dejan Popovic, Malte Scherbarth, Sébastien Tordo, Christophe Vérinaud, Julien Woillez, Sara Zuccon, Pablo Zuluaga
Items.Title: Getting the ELT into shape with the Phasing and Diagnostic Station
Items.Abstract: ESO’s Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) relies on a five-mirror design that includes a segmented 39-m primary mirror composed of 798 hexagonal segments, an adaptive flat mirror (M4), and a fast tip-tilt mirror (M5). Achieving proper alignment and phasing of the primary mirror segments—and maintaining wavefront control to within a few tens of nanometers—is essential for telescope operation.  The Phasing and Diagnostic Station (PDS) is the subsystem that provides the primary optical metrology required to bring the ELT’s mirrors into the correct shape and to enable diffraction-limited performance. The PDS will serve as the main tool for commissioning the ELT and for validating its optical performance.  To meet these objectives, the PDS hosts a versatile suite of optical sensors operating from the visible to the infrared.   We will present the operational concept of the PDS and its sensors, describe the phasing strategy, and discuss the expected performance.

Items.Authors: Jasmina Lazendic-Galloway, Maria Rita Eusébio Vale Lima, Jan Geralt bij de Vaate, Raj Rajan, Pietro Zucca, Mark Bentum, Peter Roelfsema, Wouter Laauwen, Antonio Vecchio, Christiaan Brinkering
Items.Title: L‑FIRE: A space‑based interferometric array for low‑frequency (1–40 MHz) radio astronomy
Items.Abstract: L-FIRE (Low-Frequency Interferometric Radio Explorer) is a mission concept for a spaceborne low-frequency radio interferometer operating from 1–40 MHz, a regime inaccessible from the ground. A scalable cluster of free-flying spacecraft forms a long-baseline distributed aperture using orthogonal dipole antennas and onboard correlation. The design addresses key challenges in antenna performance, formation flying, calibration, RFI mitigation, and high-volume data processing, while enabling future growth to larger constellations. L-FIRE will open a new observational window for heliospheric physics, star–planet interactions, and Galactic studies, and will deliver the first comprehensive sky survey at ultra-low radio frequencies.

Items.Authors: R. Lynne Jones, Peter Yoachim, Eric H. Neilsen, Tiago Ribeiro, Erik Dennihy, Sean MacBride
Items.Title: Scheduling the LSST: commissioning the Rubin Feature Based Scheduler
Items.Abstract: Rubin Observatory will acquire about two million science observations during the course of the ten year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). Planning these observations is the work of the Rubin Feature Based Scheduler (FBS), every 30 seconds, every twilight to twilight. The FBS has been generating simulated observations for over ten years, driving the development and co-optimization the LSST survey strategy and FBS algorithms, in a collaborative process between the project and the astronomical community under the guidance of the LSST Survey Cadence Optimization Committee (SCOC). The FBS has been in active use with the Rubin Auxiliary Telescope for several years building the framework for interactions between the FBS and summit system. The commissioning of LSSTCam in 2025 marked the first on-sky use of the FBS with the Simonyi Telescope, with an FBS configuration representative of the full LSST. We report on successes and lessons learned.

Items.Authors: Gregory J. Fetzer, Steven E. Rako, Nathan Woody, Katie Baldwin, Philip Hinz, Daren Dillon, Jeffery Roark, Elinor Gates, Juan Chilla, Celine D'Orgeville, Noelia Martinez Rey, Robert Johnson
Items.Title: On-sky demonstration of a semiconductor VECSEL-based sodium guide-star system
Items.Abstract: This presentation will address a semiconductor laser sodium guidestar system operated on sky from the Lick Observatory Shane Telescope. The speaker will discuss design, laboratory performance measurements, telescope installation (September of 2025) and subsequent operation with Shane Telescope AO systems. The system has been operated to support both system performance analysis and astronomical observations for many months.

Items.Authors: Haoran Kang, Takafumi Kojima, Takeshi Sakai, Yoichi Tamura, Shun Ishii, Akio Taniguchi, Masato Hagimoto, Masato Kato, Taku Nakajima, Tai Oshima, Sho Masui, Issei Watanabe
Items.Title: A wideband 210-350 GHz millimeter-wave receiver for LMT-FINER
Items.Abstract: The FINER project is developing two wideband dual-polarization sideband-separating receivers covering 120–210 GHz and 210–350 GHz to efficiently identify high-redshift galaxy candidates in the early universe. Based on high-Jc SIS mixer technology originally developed for the ALMA WSU, the FINER receivers are designed to provide an IF bandwidth of 3–21 GHz per sideband and per polarization, approximately five times wider than the current ALMA specifications. After installation on the LMT, these receivers are expected to offer highly efficient spectral-scanning capability among (sub)millimeter-wave facilities in the northern-hemisphere. This paper reports the initial laboratory characterization of the 210–350 GHz receiver. The measured single-sideband receiver noise temperature is approximately 100 K over most of the RF band. Digital sideband separation was also demonstrated using a wideband spectrometer array, achieving an image rejection ratio of around 20 dB in the initial tests.

Items.Authors: Shaojie Chen, Suresh Sivanandam, Olivier Lardière, Gavin Hay, Sarik Jeram, Béatrice Lessard-Hamel, Denis Brousseau, Simon Thibault, Jenny Atwood, Mark Barnet, Jiayi, Emma Xu, Saugata Dutt, Scott Christie
Items.Title: Final optical design and performance assessment of a multi-object adaptive optics-fed infrared integral-field spectrograph (GIRMOS)
Items.Abstract: We present the final end-to-end optical design of GIRMOS developed to take advantage of the adaptive optics corrected field at the Gemini North telescope. GIRMOS consists of object selection pick-offs, multi-object adaptive optics, and four identical Integral-Field Spectrographs (IFSes), which employ image slicers to arrange the integral field along a slit. The analysis shows the expected performance meets the scientific requirements and the design comply with manufacturability requirements. This paper summarizes the final optical design, engineering validation of critical components, and system performance assessment by using Structural–Thermal–Optical Performance (STOP) analysis. The results presented in this work demonstrate that GIRMOS optical design has reached a mature engineering stage and provides a solid foundation for instrument production.

Items.Authors: Michael Goodwin, Jon Lawrence, Tiger Wang, Summer Luo, Dani Guzman, Timothy Chin, Jessica Zheng, Helen McGregor, Lew Waller, Tony Farrell, Zhemin Cai, Ali Ghari Zadeh, Jon Moller, Christopher Coote, Jake Linden, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Max Hewletta, Andrew Rakich, Thierry Fusco, Delphine Barbon-Dubosc, Carlos Correia, Benoit Neichel, Pierre Jouve, Arnaud Striffling, Julien Charton, Julie Magri, Anne-Sophie Bruni Favier
Items.Title: Model-based systems engineering progress for the Gemini North Adaptive Optics Bench in critical design phase
Items.Abstract: The Gemini North Adaptive Optics Bench is a key opto-mechanical subsystem of the Gemini North Adaptive Optics facility and has completed Critical Design Review (CDR), positioning it to enter the Build Phase. This paper reports the systems engineering progress that enabled CDR success, emphasising requirements decomposition and traceability, interface management across a geographically distributed consortium, and maturation of verification and validation planning. Central to the approach is a SysML-based Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) implementation in which the system model is the authoritative source for requirements, operational concepts, architecture, and interface definition. This model-centric workflow has strengthened requirement-to-architecture traceability, supported consistent interface documentation, and improved visibility of integration and compliance risks. We conclude with the verification strategy, remaining activities, and lessons learned from applying MBSE.

Items.Authors: David Le Mignant, Coralie Neiner, Jean-Claude Bouret, Luca Fossati, Pollux Consortium
Items.Title: Pollux: high-resolution precision spectroscopy and polarimetry for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: Pollux is a proposed high-resolution spectrograph (R>75,000–100,000) with polarimetry capabilities for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, covering 100–1888 nm across five echelle spectrographs. It enables simultaneous spectroscopy and polarimetry (Stokes I, Q, U, V), addressing key science: exoplanet atmospheres, star-planet interactions, galactic evolution, and cosmic magnetic fields.   Pollux aligns with HWO’s goals, supporting studies of habitable worlds, stellar magnetism, and intergalactic media. Its design includes UV/NIR polarimeters, advanced gratings, and space-qualified detectors. This paper presents Pollux’s science objectives, instrument architecture, and development roadmap, highlighting its potential as a transformative tool for astrophysics.
